items.text: SEASON 12 · EPISODE 2 · DRAFT · CASE-061  Fenwright Group headquarters · month two · Maya, Rashida (CIO), Galen and Noor — and the finance director, who reads page one · Level L6 · Mastery support (reference only — choose the tool and say why)  The board sets aside a hundred and twenty thousand dollars a year for sixty meeting rooms. Finance has asked a simple question: is that enough? Nobody at Fenwright knows how old the rooms are.  ⚑ RV-187: the money and every acceptance of risk are the CIO's and the board's. RV-188: figures illustrative. Some choices run on a clock — and some depend on your loadout.

items.title: Lifecycle Report
items.stakes: Is $120k a year enough for sixty rooms? Nobody knows how old they are.
items.reward: A reserve with a basis, a cliff flattened, and a page the board reads every year.

objectives.text: Decide what to do about the wave

options.label: Build the lifecycle picture first with Galen and Noor: every room's install date, replacement cost and end-of-support dates — then the reserve, and the year each group of rooms ends

options.result: Double of what? The board asks. Rashida has no answer.

options.label: Ask the vendor how much they think Fenwright should spend

items.title: The cliff.
items.body: Sixty rooms at about $42,000 each to replace: $2.52 million. Over a seven-year life, R = C ÷ L gives $360,000 a year — three times the budget. But the average hides the real problem. Twenty-six rooms were installed in one wave six years ago, on one purchase order, and all reach end of life next year: 26 × $42k = $1.09 million in a single year. And a vendor letter in procurement's files says the control processors in 34 rooms lose support in fourteen months.
items.label: Test: the cliff year — and how it compares with the average.

items.alt: A bar chart of replacement cost by year for the next seven years: nothing this year, 26 rooms costing $1.09M next year in red, 14 rooms ($588k) in year three, 20 rooms ($840k) in year five; a green dashed line marks the $360k reserve and an amber one today's $120k budget.
items.caption: The average hides the cliff.

items.teaser: the purchase order from the wave
items.title: ‘26 rooms · one delivery’
items.body: The original purchase order, six years old: ‘26 rooms, complete, one delivery.’ A good price for buying everything at once. Nobody wrote down that it would all wear out at once too.

items.prompt: 26 rooms, $1.09M, next year; 34 control processors losing support. What do you recommend?
items.risk: A year the estate can't pay for.
timeout: The cliff is still there on Thursday.

hints.text: How do you turn one impossible year into several possible ones — and who accepts the wait?

options.label: Replace all 26 next year
options.result: The board can't find $1.09M in one year. Nothing is approved.

options.label: Stagger it: the 8 worst rooms this year, 10 next year, 8 deferred a year with Rashida's written acceptance — and migrate the 34 control processors before support ends
options.result: The bars flatten around the reserve line. Rashida reads the deferral twice, then signs it.
options.consequence: Flatten the cliff; the owner accepts what's deferred.

options.label: Run them until they fail
options.result: Failures arrive at the worst moments, with no money waiting.
options.consequence: A cliff you fall off one room at a time.

options.label: Replace all 26 with the cheapest rooms available
options.result: Cheaper rooms, a new standard nobody chose, and the same cliff in six years.
options.consequence: Solves the bill by breaking the standard.

items.title: Painting the bridge
items.body: For generations, ‘like painting the Forth Bridge’ meant a job that never ends: by the time the painters reached one end of the great Scottish railway bridge, opened in 1890, it was time to start again at the other. In 2011 a decade-long restoration finished with a new coating expected to last about twenty-five years. Nothing lasts forever — but you can know when it will need you next, and budget for it.

items.title: One page.
items.body: Maya's first draft is fourteen pages: every room, every model, every date. Rashida reads it in the evening and hands it back. “The finance director reads page one. That's the whole report as far as she's concerned.” So page one becomes the report: how old the estate is, what it will cost and when, what fails if nothing is done, and whose decision each line is. Three numbers, one chart, one schedule.
items.label: Test: the support share — and what goes on the page.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #113 · AVERY'S LENS  Put the future on one page before it arrives  The people with the money can only plan for what they can see: how old everything is, what replacing it costs and when, and which risks that creates — on one page, every year.  An estate bought in one wave was about to need a million dollars in one year — and the only report was fourteen pages long.

items.alt: The same chart, staggered: 8, 10, 8, 7, 7, 10 and 10 rooms a year, every bar near the green $360k reserve line. Eight rooms deferred a year with the CIO's written acceptance; the control processors migrated first.
items.caption: Flattened.

items.prompt: If I ask the board for three times the money, they'll ask why nobody said so before.

options.label: “Nobody could, before — nobody had the dates. Now you're the one who saw it a year early.”
options.reply: A year early sounds better than three times. Lead with that.

options.label: “It's what the formula says.”
options.reply: Formulas don't sit on boards. People do.

options.label: “That's not my problem.”
options.reply: It is now. It's why you're here.

items.prompt: How does the board see the estate from now on?
items.risk: The next cliff arriving as quietly as this one.
timeout: The report goes into a folder.

hints.text: What will the board need to see every year — and who presents it after you've gone?

items.note: Draft decision (DR-S12E02). Option B needs Budget at LIMITED or better.

options.label: Send the fourteen-page analysis once
options.result: Read by nobody past page one; filed.

options.label: A one-page lifecycle report every year — age, cost, risk and the schedule — with the reserve set by R = C ÷ L at $360k, presented by Rashida to the board
options.result: The board raises the reserve from next year and puts the page on every January agenda.
options.consequence: The owners see the future every year, in numbers they can act on.

options.label: Keep the $120k and ask the board to top it up whenever a room fails
options.result: Each failure becomes a special request; each request a fight.
options.consequence: The best you can do without a reserve — reactive, but honest about it.

options.label: Let Maya track it in her own spreadsheet
options.result: Accurate — until Maya leaves in ten months.
options.consequence: The future in one person's file.

items.title: ‘CP-4 · support ends in 14 months’
items.body: A vendor letter filed by procurement last spring: ‘The CP-4 control processor reaches end of support … no further firmware or security updates.’ Thirty-four rooms have one. The letter was filed under ‘vendor correspondence’.

items.alt: A meeting room at night, its display dark: NO SIGNAL; Noor, hands up; Galen pointing at the camera bar.

bubbles.text: You told me to push it to all sixty. I put it on the lab room first. The camera's gone.
It's one firmware update. It fixes the framing Teodor hates.

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  Before you say whether a budget is enough, find every thing's birthday: install dates, replacement costs, end-of-support dates. The reserve (R = C ÷ L) gives the yearly average — and hides the cliff when an estate was bought in one wave. Stagger the wave with the owner's written acceptance of whatever waits, meet support deadlines first, and put age, cost and risk on one page every year for the people who hold the money.
REFLECTION (optional)  · What in your work was bought all at once — and when will it all wear out?
